To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 0.5-300 GeV γ -ray flux of PKS 15102-089 was highly variable throughout the 3.75 year Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) observing period, undergoing several flares where the daily flux was above 10-5 photons cm-2 s-1.
we have discovered the fastest variability timescales in the γ-ray band to date for any blazar.
we have detected a new source of γ-ray emission in the Milky Way, and that this source is likely to be associated with a known pulsar wind nebula, although the exact nature is uncertain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of high-energy γ-ray emission from the flat spectrum radio source, PKS 2155-304.
the development of new methods and algorithms for the analysis of the data obtained with modern high energy gamma-ray telescopes.
understanding the physics of the emission region in the blazar class of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the γ-ray emission from the blazars PKS 1519−273 and PKS 1515−273 is not produced in the accretion disc of a super-massive black hole, but rather from relativistic jets of particles that are accelerated to relativistic velocities by shocks in the jet.

the γ-ray emission is produced by a combination of inverse Compton and external Compton scattering processes, and that the emission region has a radius of ∼10−3–10−2 light seconds and is moving relativistically with a Lorentz factor of ∼5–15.

the γ-ray emission from PKS 1512-089 is produced by inverse Compton scattering in an optically thick, relativistic jet with Doppler factor 10.5 and Lorentz factor 20, with a magnetic field of 0.1 G and an electron energy distribution that is a power-law with index -2.3, extending to a maximum Lorentz factor of 3 × 10 ^{5}.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the γ-ray emission from PKS 15101089 is dominated by the synchrotron self-Compton process.
the variability time-scale in the GeV energy band is smaller than the light travel time from the innermost regions of the jet, and the variability is likely to be produced in the jet

the variability time-scales in this object are comparable to those measured in blazar jets, which have been shown to be the emission site of the high-energy emission, and that the γ-ray emission is likely produced in the jet.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the γ-ray emission from PKS 1512−089 is variable on time-scales of less than 1 h, which is faster than the expected time-scale for light travel across the broad line region (BLR), and is consistent with variability occurring in a region smaller than the BLR.

we can constrain the size of the emission region to be smaller than ∼10−2 lt-day (assuming a Doppler factor of 10) and that we are able to constrain the magnetic field strength in the emission region to lie in the range of 10−4–10−2 G.
the γ-ray emission from PKS 1512-089 is variable on time-scales of a few hours and that the γ-ray flux can increase by more than a factor of two over a time scale of 3 hours.
